title: US Refiner Margins Hit Records as Global Fuel Shortage Squeezes Consumers at the Pump
excerpt: The 3-2-1 crack spread has reached $69.66 per barrel as refiners prioritize exports, pushing US gasoline inventories to their lowest mid-July level since 2012.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • US 3-2-1 crack spread reached a record $69.66 per barrel amid global fuel shortages.
  • Gasoline inventories fell to 210.5 million barrels, the lowest since 2012, pushing prices to $3.95 per gallon.
  • Wall Street anticipates major refiners to report profits tripling or quadrupling in Q2 2023.
  • Global refining bottlenecks caused by geopolitical issues and refinery closures are unlikely to resolve soon.

  • The US 3-2-1 crack spread — the benchmark for refiner profitability — hit a record $69.66 per barrel, its third consecutive record close, as global fuel shortages intensify.
  • US gasoline inventories have dropped to 210.5 million barrels, the lowest for mid-July since 2012, while retail gas prices have climbed to $3.95 per gallon — up 80 cents from a year ago.
  • Wall Street expects major US refiners to report profits tripling or quadrupling in the second quarter, with Valero's stock soaring 77 percent in 2026.
  • The global refining bottleneck — driven by the Iran war, Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, and years of capacity closures — has no quick fix.

A Perfect Storm for Refiners

US refining margins have surged to territory no one in the industry has seen before, and the forces driving them higher show no signs of easing. The 3-2-1 crack spread — the most widely used benchmark for refiner profitability, measuring the margin between crude oil input and refined product output — closed at $69.66 per barrel on Thursday, a record high for the third consecutive session, according to Reuters.

The numbers downstream are even more striking. The diesel crack spread settled above $91 per barrel, an all-time high. The gasoline crack spread hit roughly $59 per barrel, a level last seen during the energy crisis of June 2022, according to US Energy Information Administration data.

US refiners have become the world's supplier of last resort. As the Iran war disrupted Middle Eastern refining and exports, and Ukrainian drone strikes knocked Russian refineries offline, international buyers have turned to American fuel. US fuel exports have surged to record volumes — but that success is draining domestic stockpiles at an alarming rate.

Consumers Feel the Squeeze

"It has a gasoline problem."</p><cite>— CNN Business analysis</cite></blockquote> <p>Diesel inventories paint a similar picture."

The national average retail gasoline price stood at $3.95 per gallon on Thursday, up nearly 80 cents from the same time last year, according to GasBuddy data. Prices had spiked as high as $4.56 per gallon in May when the Strait of Hormuz blockade disrupted Middle Eastern oil exports.

The inventory picture is what worries analysts most. US gasoline stockpiles fell to 210.5 million barrels in the week ended July 10, down over 42 million barrels since late February and some 14 million barrels below the five-year seasonal average. Those levels are the lowest for this time of year since 2012 and sit just 20 million barrels above what energy consultant Andy Lipow of Lipow Oil Associates calls "critical levels."

"The world no longer has an oil problem. It has a gasoline problem."

— CNN Business analysis

Diesel inventories paint a similar picture. Though stockpiles rose 4.5 million barrels last week to about 102 million barrels, they remain nearly 11 million barrels below late February levels and 8 million barrels under the five-year seasonal average, EIA data shows.

Why the Squeeze Will Not End Soon

The global refining bottleneck is structural, not cyclical. Three forces are converging simultaneously. Middle Eastern refineries are running at reduced capacity due to the Iran war. Russia has stopped exporting diesel entirely to preserve domestic supply — a rare step for one of the world's largest fuel exporters — and is importing gasoline, an almost unprecedented reversal. And years of refinery closures across Western nations have left the global system with little spare capacity.

Building new refining capacity takes years, and no major projects are coming online anywhere in the world in the near term. Even if the Strait of Hormuz reopened tomorrow, the logistical reality favors a slow recovery: crude oil travels in supertankers carrying 2 million barrels, but refined fuels move in smaller vessels carrying tens of thousands, making the supply chain inherently slower, according to S&P Global analyst Michael Smith.

The Trump administration faces limited options. Suspending ethanol and biodiesel blending mandates — which the government raised to record levels for 2026-2027, adding an estimated 14 cents per gallon in compliance costs — could provide modest relief. But the broader global supply-demand imbalance is beyond any single policy lever.

Wall Street's Windfall

For investors, US refiners have been the clearest beneficiaries of the energy crisis. Wall Street expects Valero Energy, which reports on July 30, to post adjusted earnings of $10.13 per share on $39.5 billion in sales — a fourfold increase from the year-ago quarter's $2.28 per share. Phillips 66 is expected to triple its earnings, and Marathon Petroleum's consensus calls for adjusted EPS of $13.67, up from $3.96 a year ago.

Wall Street's Refining Boom
›Valero expected to earn $10.13 per share, up from $2.28.
›Phillips 66 projected to triple earnings.
›Marathon Petroleum's EPS forecast at $13.67, up from $3.96.
›Valero's stock surged 77% in 2026.
Wall Street earnings projections

Valero's stock has soared 77 percent in 2026, closing at record highs for five consecutive sessions before pulling back. TPH & Co. analyst Matthew Blair called the start of the July-September period "phenomenal" for US independent refiners and expects the strength to continue.

US refineries are running at 96 percent of capacity, their highest utilization rate since 2019. But encouraging refiners to shift output toward gasoline — and away from the more profitable diesel and jet fuel — will require even higher gasoline prices, independent oil analyst John Kemp wrote. For American consumers heading into the summer driving season, the implication is clear: relief at the pump is not coming anytime soon.
